summary: The machine has the tools and DocumentDB skills needed to start building the FastAPI + Beanie sample against the live Azure DocumentDB cluster. The documentdb MCP server and the DocumentDB-specific skills are present and authoritative; several cold answers were incorrect because they described the older Cosmos DB (RU) model or other neighbour services. Nothing critical is missing that would block coding, but a few clarifications and one environment permission check are needed and a few CLIs that speed infra work are absent.
summary_points: Build can start: Python, pip, git, Docker, az, the documentdb MCP server and the DocumentDB agent skills are available and sufficient to develop, test, create collections/indexes, run aggregation queries and verify the app.

Multiple cold answers incorrectly described Cosmos DB (RU) or older services — the correct resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and CLI group is az documentdb (mongocluster subcommands).

Key behavioural differences matter to code: use mongodb+srv host *.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com with tls=true and retryWrites=false; authentication supports Microsoft Entra ID (MONGODB-OIDC) as well as native users.
Local development: use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (port 10260) if running a local gateway, not a stock mongo:27017 image.
Inventory gaps: azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet and mongosh are not on PATH; mongosh is useful for manual checks but the documentdb MCP server provides nearly all data-plane validation capabilities.

tools.name: python
tools.needed_for: Run the FastAPI + Beanie sample, install dependencies, run tests and seed scripts.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or build the Python sample, install dependencies, or run the app locally.

tools.name: pip
tools.needed_for: Install packages (Beanie, motor/pymongo, FastAPI, uvicorn, python-dotenv, etc.).
tools.detail: Implied available via python on PATH.
tools.workaround: Use system package manager or container image that already has deps installed.

tools.name: az
tools.needed_for: Inspect or (optionally) provision Azure resources, retrieve cluster connection info, register provider, verify provider registration and resource provider (Microsoft.DocumentDB), list resource groups and resource types.
tools.detail: Azure CLI installed (2.89.1) and az login is signed in (subscription context available).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot inspect resource-provider registration or run the Bicep/ARM/Terraform/az resource-based deploy commands. Harder to script retrieval of connection strings and firewall rules.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server and portal for many data-plane tasks; the skill 'documentdb-azure-deployment' provides CLI examples if az becomes available later.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane operations against the target cluster: listing databases/collections, sampling documents, creating indexes, running aggregations, and explaining query plans to verify what the sample creates.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server present in inventory with 18 data-plane tools (list/aggregate/index/explain/...); connection profile 'default' is connected to the cluster per the run guidance.
tools.impact_if_missing: Majorly harder to verify indexes, aggregates, and to run explain; developer would need mongosh or direct driver connections.
tools.workaround: Use mongosh or driver-based scripts to run the same commands, but the MCP server provides convenient programmatic verification for an agent.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Fetch authoritative Microsoft docs to verify cold answers, code snippets and the correct API/CLI/resource types.
tools.detail: learn_microsoft_docs_search and related tools are available.
tools.impact_if_missing: Agent couldn't quickly ground ambiguous product naming and API differences in official docs.
tools.workaround: Manual web lookup (not recommended for agent-driven automation).

tools.name: documentdb-* skills (agent kit)
tools.needed_for: Design guidance, connection tuning, index guidance, local gateway instructions, vector and full-text search patterns, and deployment templates. These skills are the primary reference for coding and verifying the sample.
tools.detail: A broad set of documentdb-* skills are installed (documentdb-driver, -connection, -indexing, -vector-search, -azure-deployment, -local-deployment, -full-text-search, etc.).
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder would lack product-specific best-practices and code snippets; they'd have to rely on generic MongoDB advice which can be incorrect for DocumentDB-specific features.
tools.workaround: Fallback to Microsoft Learn pages, but the agent skills package the guidance and conventions needed for a quick, correct sample build.

tools.name: Docker
tools.needed_for: Optionally run the DocumentDB Gateway locally for integration tests (gateway image listens on port 10260).
tools.detail: Docker present and functioning according to inventory.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run the recommended local Gateway image for offline development; developer must test against live cluster only.
tools.workaround: Test against the live DocumentDB cluster reachable from the machine (DOCUMENTDB_URI) instead of a local gateway.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Manual interactive checks of connections, ad-hoc queries, or index troubleshooting using a Mongo shell.
tools.detail: mongosh not found on PATH per inventory.
tools.impact_if_missing: Manual interactive shell checks are less convenient; agents can still use the documentdb MCP server or write small driver scripts.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server tools for queries and aggregation, or write short Motor/PyMongo scripts to run ad-hoc checks.

tools.name: git
tools.needed_for: Source control, committing the sample, cloning templates and examples.
tools.workaround: Work without VCS or use GUI tools.

tools.name: azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet (CLIs not on PATH)
tools.needed_for: Optional: infra provisioning (Bicep/Terraform/azd) if the builder wanted to include deployment IaC as part of the sample.
tools.detail: azd, bicep, terraform and dotnet are reported as not installed in the inventory.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder cannot run the Bicep/Terraform examples locally without installing these tools; this only blocks provisioning steps which are not required by the prompt (the cluster already exists).
tools.workaround: If IaC is required, install the relevant tool(s); otherwise skip provisioning and use the provided cluster and MCP data-plane tools to verify the sample.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (i.e. a Cosmos DB account resource).
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type to create an Azure DocumentDB cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared resource-provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and the older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resource historically hosted MongoDB API endpoints; both use the DocumentDB provider name but they are different resource types (databaseAccounts vs mongoClusters).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts in templates or CLI calls they would create or target the Cosmos DB account resource (RU-based) instead of the vCore-based DocumentDB cluster; CLI/Bicep commands, API versions and resource properties would be wrong and deployments would fail or create the wrong service.
improvements: On the Azure DocumentDB Quickstart and deployment pages (e.g., Quickstart: Bicep), add a prominent sentence: 'Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (az documentdb mongocluster) — do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts which targets Cosmos DB accounts.'
Add a deprecation/clarification notice on older databaseAccounts Bicep/ARM samples that target MongoDB to point readers to mongoClusters for vCore DocumentDB.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group. Example: az cosmosdb create ... (az cosmosdb is part of the core az CLI, not an extra extension.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Use az documentdb mongocluster subcommands (e.g. az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster show / az documentdb mongocluster list) or az resource create against Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters. The CLI supports az documentdb mongocluster commands in the core az CLI (not the legacy az cosmosdb group for this resource).

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (Azure CLI docs)
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both services expose MongoDB APIs under the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider and older Cosmos DB docs still reference az cosmosdb; the similar naming (cosmosdb vs documentdb) is a common source of error.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb mongocluster create (older/other CLI pages)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create or the wrong command group would either fail or manage Cosmos DB resources instead of the desired mongoClusters, leading to mis-deployment or wrong API behaviour.
improvements: Update the CLI quickstarts and the top-level 'Create cluster' quickstart to explicitly show az documentdb mongocluster create examples and add a short 'Not az cosmosdb' note.
Add example az documentdb list-connection-strings usage in the Python quickstart README so sample builders use the correct CLI path.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account (MongoDB kind).
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/Terraform resource type for Azure DocumentDB clusters is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters. Terraform (AzureRM) exposes this via azurerm_mongo_cluster (or via AzAPI/azurerm provider modules referencing Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters). Do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account for vCore DocumentDB clusters.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Old Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) templates historically held MongoDB 'kind' and Terraform modules for Cosmos appear similar; the product rename and the introduction of mongoClusters created overlapping terminology.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts in Bicep/Terraform they would target a different service model (RU-based Cosmos DB) and the deployed resource would not be the intended vCore-based DocumentDB cluster.
improvements: Add clear Bicep/Terraform examples for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters on the main quickstart page and in the Terraform module registry examples; add a migration note on pages that still show databaseAccounts for 'Mongo' examples.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false (mongodb:// with port 10255 and replicaSet=globaldb).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters use mongodb+srv scheme for cluster endpoints; host form is <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (or <cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com for single-cluster). Recommended options include tls=true (or tls param in driver), retryWrites=false, maxIdleTimeMS=120000, and for Microsoft Entra ID auth use authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC (or configure OIDC properties). The SRV form is the documented default for connecting to clusters.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the older CosmosDB Mongo-compatible endpoint style (host *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and explicit port 10255) which many Cosmos quickstarts used; the newer vCore DocumentDB cluster expects SRV endpoints and has slightly different hostnames and recommended options.

confusion_sources.title: Example Cosmos DB Mongo connection strings (older Cosmos docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong connection string form (wrong host / wrong port / missing MONGODB-OIDC options) can cause connection failures, authentication errors, or incorrect routing to a different service endpoint.
improvements: Add a short 'connection string for apps' snippet to the sample README showing the exact recommended SRV URI and mandatory query options (tls=true, retryWrites=false, authMechanism/MONGODB-OIDC example).
On Learn pages that show older Cosmos DB Mongo examples, add a highlighted note when readers should use mongodb+srv and the mongoClusters host for vCore DocumentDB.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is typically provisioned as Azure Cosmos DB throughput measured in Request Units (RUs) (provisioned or autoscale).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB uses a vCore/compute-tier + storage billing model (cluster tiers M10..M200 etc.) — you pick a compute tier (vCores/memory per shard) and storage per shard. It is not RU-based; the RU model applies to Azure Cosmos DB (RU-based) offerings.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both DocumentDB and Cosmos DB are managed by the same Microsoft provider namespace historically and 'Cosmos DB' is often discussed in the same contexts; many writers assume RU billing for any Cosmos-branded database and conflate the two offerings.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB RU-based throughput docs

confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes RU-based throughput they may choose the wrong cluster sizing, pick the wrong API or try to create throughput policies that the vCore cluster doesn't accept, leading to provisioning or performance misconfigurations.
improvements: Update quickstarts and migration guidance to prominently state 'Azure DocumentDB uses compute tiers (M10..M200) + storage — not RU-based throughput' and include a one-line cost-model comparison.
Add a sample sizing note in the sample's README linking to the pricing page and recommending M30 for prod-like workloads as in the deployment skill.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB drivers normally authenticate with SCRAM username/password; AAD token-based auth for the MongoDB API is not commonly used — use SCRAM credentials in the connection string.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native (SCRAM-like native users/keys) and Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication. For Entra ID you can connect using MONGODB-OIDC / OIDC parameters (mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC&...) or use managed identities with appropriate driver callbacks. The service documents examples for using Entra ID/OIDC with MongoDB drivers and with tools (Compass, mongosh) and for service-to-service scenarios.
confusions.grounding_source: learn_microsoft_docs_search (Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID)

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Azure Cosmos DB's Mongo API used only username/password and resource tokens; the new vCore DocumentDB service added OIDC/Microsoft Entra ID support which older guidance may omit.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos/Mongo guidance focusing on username/password

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only SCRAM credentials are supported they will miss the opportunity to use managed identities or Entra-based auth in environments where that is required by security policy. Conversely, using OIDC without following the documented driver pattern will fail to authenticate.
improvements: Add a short 'how to use OIDC with Motor / PyMongo' snippet to the Python quickstart (the Beanie tutorial already shows an OIDC callback pattern) and link to the Entra auth doc.
Add an explicit 'supported auth methods' block at the top of connection quickstarts to prevent readers assuming only SCRAM is possible.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers. For Python async + Beanie use Motor and Beanie. There is no separate MongoDB-specific Azure SDK.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the regular MongoDB drivers. For Python async stacks, Motor (AsyncIOMotorClient) is the right driver and Beanie is suitable as the ODM. There is no separate DocumentDB-specific application SDK for MongoDB API access — use the MongoDB drivers.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: DiskANN, HNSW, IVF; use db.collection.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536, ... } }) — approximate createIndex form.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a native vector-search feature surfaced as the 'cosmosSearch' search index family; the vector subtypes include vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, and vector-ivf. Indexes and definitions are created with the createSearchIndexes database command (or the service's search-index creation API), and queries use the $search aggregation stage with 'cosmosSearch' rather than the community createIndex vector syntax.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Community or Atlas-style createIndex/vector syntax differs from DocumentDB's 'createSearchIndexes' + $search + 'cosmosSearch' approach; the cold answer used a generic MongoDB-style createIndex pattern that doesn't reflect DocumentDB's 'cosmosSearch' commands.

confusion_sources.title: Atlas / some community vector index examples (createIndex style)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses mongo createIndex vector syntax the index creation will fail or the index will not be created as intended; vector queries will not return expected results.
improvements: Document the exact createSearchIndexes payload for a sample vector index in both the sample's seed script and the Beanie quickstart, and include a 'how to migrate Atlas vector syntax to DocumentDB cosmosSearch index' snippet.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB text indexes ($text) or integrate Azure Cognitive Search for richer/hybrid vector+text retrieval.
confusions.grounded_answer: On Azure DocumentDB, use the built-in full-text search via createSearchIndexes and query using the $search aggregation stage (BM25 scoring). For hybrid (lexical + vector) retrieval, DocumentDB supports combining BM25 ($search) and vector search (cosmosSearch) on the same collection; you should prefer DocumentDB's native search functionality over community $text indexes for richer results.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many MongoDB-based tutorials rely on the $text operator and text indexes; DocumentDB provides a richer built-in search engine and a different index creation API (createSearchIndexes), so $text is a community pattern not preferred here.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses $text and the standard createIndex text approach, they will miss DocumentDB features (BM25, analyzers, hybrid vector+text) and may implement suboptimal search that is inconsistent with the product's recommendations.
improvements: Add a short sample createSearchIndexes JSON and a sample $search pipeline to the Python sample's README demonstrating fuzzy and phrase search and an RRF-style hybrid combination with vector search.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: The MongoDB wire protocol version depends on the selected compatibility version; recent accounts can support MongoDB 6.0/7.0 depending on compatibility. Some server-side JS and admin commands may be unsupported.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore, MongoDB-compatible) supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, and 8.0 (depending on cluster serverVersion selection) and implements ~99% of common MongoDB operators. Some admin and low-level commands or specific engine internals may not be exposed; check the product compatibility page for exact operator coverage for edge-case commands.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB FAQ (compatibility and supported MongoDB versions)

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a standard MongoDB Docker image (mongo:7.0) on port 27017 for local development because the Cosmos emulator lacks full Mongo support.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB local development the recommended image is the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712). Use the Gateway image and follow the local-connection-config guidance (TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256) rather than a stock mongo:27017 image to get product parity.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: General MongoDB advice uses a stock mongo image for local dev; DocumentDB provides a Gateway image with product-specific behaviour and recommended TLS/port/credentials (port 10260), which many community posts do not mention.
confusions.build_risk: Testing against a stock mongo:27017 image will miss platform-specific behaviours (TLS, SCRAM config, embedded search/vector features) and produce false positive results for the sample's integration tests.
improvements: Add 'local dev' callouts to the sample README pointing to the Gateway image and docker-compose snippet, including the exact port 10260, TLS guidance and SKIP_INIT_DATA flags.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported only if the account's MongoDB API compatibility level includes the server features; confirm in account settings. No special flag usually required.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams. For multishard clusters or some preview capabilities you may need to enable the 'Change streams for multishard clusters' feature in the cluster settings; otherwise change streams are available for accounts with compatible serverVersion and driver support.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The service-specific MCP server is 'documentdb' and the azure MCP server does not provide DocumentDB-specific collection/index inspection tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane inspection (the inventory includes it). The Azure MCP server is useful for control-plane lookups but does not replace the DocumentDB data-plane tools for aggregation, explain, index creation, etc.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft's DocumentDB was the original name of the proprietary JSON document database service that later became Azure Cosmos DB; Microsoft DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is unrelated to any separate open-source 'DocumentDB' project.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong: the new service 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' is the rebranding of the vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB offering (the team renamed that vCore Cosmos offering). The historical original 'DocumentDB' (2014–2017) became Azure Cosmos DB; the current Azure DocumentDB product is distinct and is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine. So the relationships are: (1) the original 'DocumentDB' name migrated to Cosmos DB in the past; (2) 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore)' is the renamed vCore Cosmos offering and is now a separate product; (3) the service is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?
Azure DocumentDB FAQ (relation to Cosmos DB)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The product naming history is complex and the same 'DocumentDB' label has been used at different times for different things (original DocumentDB → Cosmos DB; 'vCore' Cosmos DB for MongoDB → renamed to Azure DocumentDB), causing overlap in older docs and blog posts.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB historical docs referencing 'DocumentDB'

confusions.build_risk: Naming confusion could cause builders to pick the wrong target API or resource type (deploying databaseAccounts vs mongoClusters) or copy old connection/CLI examples that don't apply to the vCore-based product.
improvements: Add a single-line 'Naming history' box at the top of the main Azure DocumentDB overview and Quickstart pages clarifying: 'Azure DocumentDB (this product) = previously Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore). The original DocumentDB (2014–2017) became Azure Cosmos DB — these are separate things.'
Add a 'Which resource type to use' table on the overview showing Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters vs Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts and when to use each.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB API the underlying engine is Azure Cosmos DB's proprietary multi-model engine.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore Mongo-compatible offering) is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the microsoft/documentdb project). From application code you use standard MongoDB drivers, but expect DocumentDB-specific differences in admin commands, some engine-level behaviours, and the service's integrated search/vector features — you should test compatibility for edge-case admin commands.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (overview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB's historical branding and the reuse of the 'DocumentDB' name for different products leads to assumptions the engine is Cosmos's proprietary core, but the vCore offering is explicitly built on the open-source DocumentDB engine.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming the wrong engine could lead developers to rely on Cosmos-only admin commands or to misinterpret behaviour around indexing, backups and vector/text search features.
improvements: Add an explicit 'engine' line to the product overview and quickstarts: 'Azure DocumentDB uses the open-source DocumentDB engine (link) — the runtime is not the same as the Cosmos DB Core engine.'

confusions.question: Which database name should the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_retail_15 for everything the sample creates and queries.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run environment in the sample description explicitly instructs to use database 'sample_retail_15'.

confusions.question: How should the Python app create the Motor client from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI?
confusions.cold_answer: Instantiate Motor directly from the env var: client = AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']); db = client['sample_retail_15']
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: create AsyncIOMotorClient using the DOCUMENTDB_URI from the environment and pick the sample_retail_15 database. Ensure the URI contains the recommended options (tls=true/retryWrites=false) or pass them as client options. The documentdb-driver skill recommends a singleton client for reuse.

confusions.question: How to initialize Beanie with Motor and the Pydantic document models?
confusions.cold_answer: Use init_beanie with the Motor database and the document model list: await init_beanie(database=db, document_models=[Supplier, PurchaseOrder])
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the Beanie quickstart shows exactly this pattern (pass the Motor database object and the list of document models to init_beanie).

confusions.question: What indexes should the sample create for suppliers and purchase orders?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a unique index for supplier code/name on suppliers and indexes on purchase_orders for supplier_id and status.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct and aligned with DocumentDB indexing guidance: create a unique index for a supplier identifier (code or name) on suppliers, and create single-field indexes on purchase_orders for supplier_id and status to support join/aggregation patterns. DocumentDB indexing skill also recommends compound/index shapes per query patterns.

confusions.question: What aggregation pipeline will summarise open PO value by supplier (what exact stages)?
confusions.cold_answer: Pipeline: match status=open → group by supplier_id summing total → lookup from suppliers → unwind → project supplier_id, supplier_name, open_value, count.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: That aggregation pipeline is the right approach for summarising open PO value by supplier; it matches on status, groups by supplier_id, sums total fields, performs a $lookup into suppliers, unwinds the supplier and projects the final fields. Use the documentdb-natural-language-querying best-practices (filter early, ensure indexes on match fields) to keep the pipeline efficient.

information_gaps.title: Permissions on provided DOCUMENTDB_URI
information_gaps.description: The inventory and skills confirm a cluster is reachable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) and the documentdb MCP profile 'default' is connected, but no skill or doc in the inventory states whether the credentials available to the developer (DOCUMENTDB_URI) permit creating collections, indexes and roles. The builder must verify at runtime whether the connection string grants admin-level permissions or only read access; check via documentdb_list_databases or attempt a safe index-list call.

information_gaps.title: Which fields are authoritative for Supplier / PurchaseOrder schema
information_gaps.description: The prompt left exact field names/types unspecified. Several skills provide modelling guidance but there is no single authoritative schema for the sample. The builder must decide required fields (e.g., supplier.name, supplier.code, supplier.contact, purchase_order.supplier_id, total (decimal/float), status enum) or request the author to supply the canonical schema.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (az documentdb mongocluster) as the resource type for cluster operations; do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts which targets Cosmos DB (RU model).

Connect with the SRV-style URI (mongodb+srv) to the cluster host <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and include tls=true and retryWrites=false; when using Microsoft Entra ID authentication, use authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and follow the Entra/OIDC examples.

sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

guidance_for_builder.instruction: For local development use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (port 10260) and follow the gateway TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256 guidance rather than using a stock mongo:latest image to preserve feature parity with the managed cluster.

Create a singleton AsyncIOMotorClient from DOCUMENTDB_URI and init Beanie with await init_beanie(database=client["sample_retail_15"], document_models=[Supplier, PurchaseOrder]) on application startup; follow Beanie quickstart dependency versions shown in the official quickstart.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample: the cluster already exists and az (Azure CLI) is available for any control-plane checks. Install azd only if the builder plans to add azd-driven repo templates or app deployments.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install bicep if the sample will include Bicep deployment files or if the builder wants to validate Bicep templates locally; otherwise not required because the cluster already exists. Install with: 'az bicep install' or follow the Bicep install docs.

references.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install Terraform only if the sample will ship Terraform IaC (azurerm provider + azurerm_mongo_cluster or AzAPI modules). If not provisioning, the agent can skip it; otherwise install Terraform and the AzureRM provider.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not necessary for a Python FastAPI + Beanie sample. Add only if the developer intends to provide a .NET sample or test harness.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh for convenient interactive troubleshooting and manual index/aggregate checks. If not available, the documentdb MCP server and short Motor/PyMongo scripts can perform equivalent checks programmatically. Install mongosh from the MongoDB download pages or 'npm i -g mongosh'.

references.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (Compass/mongosh examples)
